items.title: US Democratic senator introduces bill to end China's trade status ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US Democratic Senator Tammy Baldwin on Tuesday introduced legislation to revoke China's normal trade status and favorable tariff treatment just days before US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to meet for a third time this year to discuss a delicate trade truce.

Baldwin's bill, which argues that Beijing had failed to uphold the principles of fair trade, would set a deadline to end the permanent normal trade relations that have been in effect since 2002 a year after the legislation is enacted.

The legislation, which could have more support under a Congress controlled by Democrats next year, would shift Chinese imports to higher regular US tariff rates under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule.

The existing US "Most Favored Nation" tariff rates for China and other countries average about 2.5%, but Trump has heaped punitive duties on Chinese imports, about 25% during his first term and up to 20% during his second term under a trade truce with Beijing.

Baldwin's bill also would direct the US Trade Representative's office to issue a report together with the Commerce Department and US International Trade Commission and other bodies on ongoing trade and economic challenges posed by China.

Lawmakers have repeatedly sought to revoke China's special treatment in recent years, but the bills have failed due to competing economic priorities, legislative bottlenecks, and shifting trade dynamics, with Republicans not challenging Trump's tariff pressure. But there is growing anti-China sentiment in Congress, particularly among Democrats who won control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in elections this month.

Trump, who meets with Xi in Shenzhen, China, this week, could still veto the bill if it passes.

"We need to reset our trade relationship with China, be honest that they have undercut us at every turn, and put the focus back where it matters — prioritizing American workers, manufacturers and families," said Baldwin, who voted against the change in China's tariff treatment in 2000 while serving in the House of Representatives.

She said in a statement that the US had "rolled out the red carpet for China" for two decades while Beijing had engaged in market manipulation, intellectual property theft and other unfair trade practices, noting that the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent, bipartisan legislative agency, also recommended revoking the PNTR status of China in November 2024.

Western concerns about China's efforts to dominate global markets have grown in recent years, fueled by Beijing's threats to shut off exports of critical minerals needed for advanced manufacturing — and its actual moves to do so for Japan.

Trump, who ordered a review of China's trade status when he took office in January 2025, and Xi are expected to discuss a fragile trade-war truce that will expire in January when they meet later this week amid growing tensions over trade. China's foreign ministry has accused the US of "economic coercion" over its latest restrictions on Chinese access to advanced chips.

Baldwin's office said there was "growing recognition that granting China PNTR failed to deliver the changes in China's economic and trade practices that were promised," and the bill would establish a more durable US trade policy.

Revoking China's current trade status would increase the price of Chinese imports, especially for manufactured goods, and in the long run, raise US consumer prices by 0.7% and reduce US economic output by 0.2%, the US International Trade Commission said in a 319-page report released in August.

But two ITC commissioners — a Republican and a Democrat — challenged the notion that ending PNTR status for China would raise costs, arguing that the analysis failed to account for economic harm caused by granting it in the first place.

The ITC concluded that revoking PNTR would raise trade-weighted average tariffs by 35.2 percentage points.

items.title: US official says recent tech woes not tied to cyberattacks
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - A recent series of US technology outages is not tied to cyberattacks but rather to aging computer systems that are in need of upgrades, the country's top homeland security official said on Tuesday.

Disruptions at United Airlines (UAL.O), the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft (MSFT.O) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) have raised alarm.

"Some of the technology that they're pushing out there, they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system," Markwayne Mullin told CNBC. "But it has nothing to do with cyberattacks, and I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out."

Mullin said maybe companies needed to start telling customers before conducting a scheduled upgrade and warn them of possible disruptions for a short period of time.

"I can tell you 98% certainty this isn't a cyberattack," he added.

Mullin said that at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday there would be a long-scheduled test of the emergency alert system. Radio and television broadcasters nationwide will interrupt normal programming to relay a one-minute test message.

The FAA issued a nearly five-hour ground stop on Friday that led to airlines cancelling more than 18,000 flights over three days in the longest outage since the September 11, 2001, attacks. The outage was blamed on the installation of a single router in a remote facility in Arkansas.

United said a computer problem on Monday forced a halt to many departing flights, while JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, on Monday experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug but said there was no evidence it was cyber-related.

Microsoft on Saturday said services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours. Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident and it was not aware of any malicious activity.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Nia Williams

items.title: US retail sales showcase underlying strength despite cost-of-living crunch
items.content_html:
• Retail sales increase 0.2% in October, in line with economists' expectations
  • Core retail sales rise 0.6%; September sales gain revised up to 0.5% from 0.1%
  • Import prices advance 1.1%, exceed economists' expectations for a 0.7% increase
  • Manufacturing production increases 0.3%, with strong gains in AI-related segments

WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - US retail sales increased moderately in October as households pulled back on purchases of motor vehicles and furniture, but maintained spending elsewhere, keeping the economy on solid footing at the start of the fourth quarter.

The report from the Commerce Department on Tuesday also showed upward revisions to so-called core retail sales, which exclude motor vehicles among other categories, in September.

Spending has remained resilient despite rising inflation eroding purchasing power for mostly lower- and middle-income households.

The underlying strength in retail sales, together with other data on Tuesday showing a bigger-than-expected increase in import prices last month, reinforced economists' views that the Federal Reserve would continue raising interest rates after next month's widely expected hike.

"More consumers are clearly struggling with rapidly rising prices but are not yet ready to throw in the towel," said Scott Anderson, chief US economist at BMO Capital Markets.

"Instead, consumers appear to be strategically allocating their monthly budgets to stretch their dollars into different categories every month. While under some pressure, real consumer spending is expected to perform well enough in the fourth quarter to keep the Fed focused on its inflation mandate."

Retail sales rose 0.2% last month after an unrevised 0.8% surge in September, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said. The increase was in line with economists' expectations. Retail sales are mostly goods and are not adjusted for inflation. They gained 6.8% on a year-on-year basis in October.

The ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up inflation, outpacing wage growth. The government reported last month that income at the disposal of households after adjusting for inflation and taxes fell 0.3% in September.

Some economists said the retail sales share of consumer spending was shrinking, which they attributed to the bifurcation of the household sector, with the rising cost of living disproportionately hurting middle- and lower-income households.

"They tend to spend more of their income on physical goods, such as food and clothing, and squeezed spending power limits the potential for growth," said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING.

"High-income households have seen their wealth surge, boosting consumption, and are accounting for a growing share of total consumer spending. However, they spend more of their income on services and experiences, such as leisure, hospitality and travel, which are not included in retail sales."

The ongoing technology-led selloff could temper spending by making consumers more cautious.

Retail sales last month were held back by a 1.6% decline in receipts at auto dealers. Sales at furniture retailers fell 2.3%, while receipts at electronics and appliance stores were unchanged. There were decreases in sales at clothing retailers as well as at sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument and book stores.

But building material store sales increased 0.5%, and there were strong rises in receipts at service stations as well as health and personal care outlets. Sales at nonstore retailers jumped 1.2%, likely reflecting Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days promotion. Sales at miscellaneous store retailers, including florists and pet stores, soared 4.7%.

Receipts at food services and drinking places, the only services component in the report, rose 0.2%.

GROWTH ESTIMATES REVISED UP

Retail sales excluding automobiles, gasoline, building materials and food services increased 0.6% last month after an upwardly revised 0.5% rise in September. Economists had forecast these core retail sales, which correspond most closely with the consumer spending component of gross domestic product, advancing 0.4% after a previously reported 0.1% gain in September.

That led economists to temper their expectations for a slowdown in consumer spending this quarter after growing at a 3.8% annualized rate for two straight quarters. Economists at Goldman Sachs raised their fourth-quarter GDP growth estimate by 0.6 percentage point to a 2.4% annualized rate.

The economy grew at a 3.4% pace in the July-September quarter, fueled by both consumer spending and business investment in AI, though signs are pointing to an upgrade when the government publishes its second estimate next week.

Stocks on Wall Street fell, with the Nasdaq Composite index hitting an eight-month low. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

A separate report from the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics showed import prices increased 1.1% in October after rising by the same margin in September.

Economists had forecast import prices, which exclude tariffs, climbing 0.7%. The BLS did not publish year-over-year import price readings because last year's federal government shutdown prevented the collection of data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Imported inflation accelerated 8.1% in September, the largest gain in just over four years.

The government last week reported stronger-than-expected consumer prices in October as well as firmer producer inflation details. Financial markets have priced in a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December and anticipated another increase in borrowing costs in January, CME's FedWatch tool showed.

The US central bank left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. Import prices were last month driven by fuels, capital goods related to AI, motor vehicles, engines and parts as well as consumer goods.

International airfares also increased. This component goes into the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, excluding food and energy, one of the inflation measures tracked by the Fed for its 2% target.

Economists continued to believe that so-called core PCE inflation increased 0.3% for the third straight month in October. In the 12 months through October, they forecast core PCE inflation advancing 3.2% after rising 3.1% in September.

AI-related investment underpinned manufacturing, with a third report from the Fed showing factory production rising 0.3% for a second consecutive month in October. Economists expected the trend to persist despite growing backlash to data centers and regulation fears following the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in this month's midterm elections.

"Policy at the state and local level will slow and prolong, not derail, the buildout," said Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics.

"A bigger risk, though, is that with inflation stubbornly elevated and the labor market showing signs of re-acceleration, the Fed presses even harder on the brakes, uncovering vulnerabilities in the most leveraged parts of the AI ecosystem and causing a sharper pullback in AI-driven spending."

items.title: Trump approval holds near career low at 32%, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's approval rating held near the lowest level of his presidency, while the leader of the Democrats in the US Senate also showed signs he was losing popularity within his party on the eve of a leadership challenge, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

The four-day poll showed 32% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in the White House, a rate that has held steady in four straight Reuters/Ipsos polls since mid-October when the president's rating was 31%, a career low.

Trump's popularity has tumbled this year as the US war with Iran has hit Americans' personal finances by pushing fuel prices sharply higher, an economic conflagration that cost Trump's Republican Party control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. Just 31% of Americans support the war in Iran, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

SOUR ON SCHUMER

The poll showed Democratic respondents divided about the party's leadership in Congress, with more viewing Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer unfavorably than viewing him favorably. The party's House leader, Hakeem Jeffries, was viewed more favorably than unfavorably within his party.

Some 34% of self-identified Democrats in the poll said they have a favorable view of Schumer, who is facing a leadership challenge from fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Some 43% of Democrats in the poll said they had an unfavorable view of Schumer, while 22% said they had never heard of him.

In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in February, 38% of Democrats said they looked on Schumer favorably and 37% viewed him unfavorably.

Van Hollen has been more forceful in criticizing Israel's war in Gaza, arguing that blocks on some weapons sales to Israel might be needed. Schumer has also criticized Israel's attacks on Gaza but has voted against limits on weapons sales to the US ally.

Israel's war in Gaza, which has leveled vast swaths of the occupied territory following deadly attacks in 2023 by Palestinian militants on Israeli civilians, has sharply divided Democrats, eroding the longstanding support for Israel within the party.

Democratic lawmakers will take control of the US Senate and House of Representatives in January.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll also found that Jeffries was better liked than Schumer, with 40% of Democrats looking on him favorably and 29% unfavorably, with 29% saying they don't know the name.

Republicans are more united around their leadership, with 75% saying they like Trump and 77% saying the same of Vice President JD Vance.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, surveyed 1,521 US adults nationwide and had a margin of error of about 3 percentage points.

Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; additional reporting by Tim Reid; editing by Scott Malone and Deepa Babington

items.title: United Airlines says technology outage that delayed departures has been resolved
items.content_html:
CHICAGO, Nov 16 (Reuters) - United Airlines (UAL.O) said on Monday it had resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures for about an hour, just days after a nationwide air traffic control outage caused widespread disruption to US airlines.

The disruption, which ended around 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), highlighted how computer failures can ground flights even when aircraft and crews are ready to depart.

There was no indication that United's outage was connected to Friday's Federal Aviation Administration shutdown, which caused the longest nationwide ground stop of departing flights since the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States.

"This is not an FAA system-wide problem," US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an interview on Monday on Fox News' "Hannity" show. "I don't know what the root cause of United is," he added.

United said a technology issue that delayed flight departures had been resolved, adding that flights already airborne and those operated by United Express had been unaffected throughout.

"There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," the airline said.

An internal memo from United's pilots union, seen by Reuters, said a companywide web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications.

The memo said United had been unable to provide final aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates. Such information is essential for pilots to complete pre-departure calculations.

In a subsequent memo, the union said United's systems were coming back online and directed pilots to check updated company communications.

Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday's outage involved United's Unimatic system.

Alaska Airlines (ALK.N) also briefly halted departures nationwide in April 2024 after a problem with its weight-and-balance system.

FLIGHT DISRUPTIONS

As of 6:50 p.m. ET (2350 GMT), United had delayed 645 flights, or 20% of its schedule, and canceled 25 on Monday, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. It was unclear how many of those disruptions were caused by Monday's technology issue, as airlines were still recovering from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop.

United shares went down 2.5% in after-hours trading.

Some passengers reported on social media that their aircraft had returned to the gate after reaching the runway.

The outage came as US air travel was largely returning to normal following Friday's nationwide ground stop, which lasted nearly five hours after a failure in the FAA's telecommunications network.

More than 18,100 flights scheduled to depart US airports between Friday and Sunday were canceled or had not taken off within three hours of their scheduled departure times, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. Not all were necessarily affected by the FAA outage.

items.title: US Supreme Court sidesteps fight over Maryland's 'sensitive places' gun curbs
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to decide whether a Maryland law banning the carry of guns in certain "sensitive places" such as stadiums, bars and public parks violates constitutional gun rights.

The justices turned away an appeal by gun rights advocates of a lower court's decision finding that the restrictions comport with the US Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and bear arms."

Maryland was one of several states to enact new restrictions on the carrying of firearms in locations deemed "sensitive" after a landmark Supreme Court ruling in 2022 expanded gun rights.

Maryland's law, signed in 2023 by Democratic Governor Wes Moore, prohibited guns in such locations as college campuses, hospitals, power plants, amusement parks and places that sell alcohol or cannabis for on-site consumption. These built on Maryland's longstanding gun-carry restrictions in locations that include public transit, casinos, schools and public protest sites.

THE BRUEN TEST

Gun rights groups, including the Second Amendment Foundation, and several firearms-owning residents sued to challenge the law. They argued that a number of the state's location-based restrictions violated their Second Amendment rights as defined by the Supreme Court's 2022 decision in the case New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen.

The Bruen ruling declared for the first time that the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to carry a handgun in public for self-defense. It was one of three key rulings by the Supreme Court since 2008 that broadened gun rights in a nation deeply divided over how to address firearms violence including frequent mass shootings. The United States has the world's highest gun ownership rate.

Under a legal test set out in the Bruen decision, gun control measures must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" — not simply advance an important government interest — in order to comply with the Second Amendment. The challengers in the Maryland case argued that the state's restrictions failed the Bruen test.

A federal judge in 2023 upheld some location-based restrictions while blocking others, prompting separate appeals by gun rights groups challenging the law and Maryland officials defending it. On appeal, the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals approved all of Maryland's disputed location bans. This led to the current appeal to the Supreme Court.

JUSTICE THOMAS WEIGHS IN

Conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, who authored the Bruen ruling, in a statement attached to Monday's order said he was skeptical that Maryland's restrictions are lawful. But Thomas agreed with the decision to turn away the case, saying the broad challenge by the plaintiffs would complicate the court's review.

"In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of states' authority to ban firearms in 'sensitive places,'" Thomas wrote.

The Second Amendment Foundation expressed disappointment but noted that its challenge to New York's firearm restrictions in public parks is also pending before the court.

"We are hopeful the court takes a very hard look at that case and elects to restore the right to carry for the Americans all over the country that are subject to these unconstitutional laws," foundation official Bill Sack said.

The court further expanded gun rights in a pair of decisions this year. In a 6-3 ruling powered by its conservative majority, the court in June struck down a Hawaii law that required gun owners to get an owner's permission before bringing a handgun onto private property open to the public, such as most businesses.

The justices also decided unanimously in June to limit the application of a decades-old federal law that bars firearms possession by certain drug users, narrowing a measure that had threatened the gun rights of millions of Americans who use marijuana and own firearms.

The decisions reinforced the Bruen test that gun control measures must clear in order to survive scrutiny under the amendment, ratified in 1791. The provision states, "A well regulated militia, being necessary to the security of a free state, the right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed."

The court on December 2 will hear a challenge to the legality of state restrictions on assault-style rifles, giving the justices another chance to expand gun rights in a case that involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings.

Reporting by John Kruzel; Additional reporting by Andrew Chung; Editing by Will Dunham

items.title: US must intensify vaccination effort to regain measles-free status lost after 26 years
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON/CHICAGO, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Public health experts say the US must drive vaccinations and disease surveillance in order to regain the hard-won measles-free status it held for 26 years that a Trump administration official said on Monday had been revoked.

The Pan American Health Organization told the Trump administration in a letter on Friday that the United States had lost the status, the official said. PAHO is expected to make the formal announcement on Tuesday.

The decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.

About 7,700 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.

Regaining measles elimination status requires demonstrating that measles transmission has stopped and is not sustained for 12 months, and that the country has a high-quality, functioning surveillance system.

But measles outbreaks continue to appear in places like Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin, with no clear evidence that transmission has ended nationally, said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University. She said it is unlikely that all measles cases were being counted.

In its letter, PAHO urged the US to intensify its vaccination efforts to halt transmission of the highly contagious virus, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a decision that is not yet public.

"What we need to do is terminate the current transmission. To do that, we need to enhance immunization uptake in virtually all communities," said Walter Orenstein, a professor emeritus at Emory University.

Orenstein was a member of the US independent advisory panel that presented the CDC's measles status report along with its assessment that the US had likely lost its measles elimination status to PAHO in a meeting last week.

DECLINING VACCINATION RATES, GROWING MISTRUST

Public trust in vaccination fell during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and messaging from Kennedy and the White House about the risks of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine has exacerbated those concerns, several experts said.

While the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said it supports vaccinations for measles, the government has put millions of dollars into investigating vaccine safety and publicly pushed several states to loosen school vaccine mandates.

"Regaining that trust takes time, and requires a consistent effort from the officials that are working in public health," said Josh Michaud, a public health analyst with KFF, a health policy research group.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz, who has been in the job for three months, told Reuters last week that if the US loses elimination status, the agency would not change its response.

Two shots of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at stopping the spread of measles. WHO recommends that 95% of people receive two shots of the vaccine in order to achieve herd immunity, which can protect those unable to be vaccinated and prevent spread.

In August, the CDC reported that vaccination coverage among children in kindergarten in the 2025-26 school year was 92.4%, but in certain pockets of the United States the coverage is much lower. During the South Carolina measles outbreak earlier this year, some individual schools in Spartanburg County reported immunization rates as low as 20%.

Dr. Ben Kasstan-Dabush, assistant professor of global health & development at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said the US needs to increase vaccinations across all groups.

As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the CDC to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States for 12 months or longer. The senior administration official said the outbreak in Utah, which began in June 2025, was key to PAHO's determination.

Other critical tools needed to improve the US response include improving surveillance networks to be able to identify and test for the virus and beefing up epidemiological capacity to follow up on cases and interrupt chains of transmission.

Orenstein said it is critical that the United States resume its support for global immunization efforts, which were disrupted when the US dropped out of the World Health Organization.

He said every US measles case in the past two years originated as an imported virus, often brought in by Americans traveling abroad who then sparked local outbreaks.

Reporting by Yasmeen Abutaleb; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama, Caroline Humer and Bill Berkrot

items.title: New York Mayor Mamdani disbands 'notorious' police unit that used excessive force on protesters
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 16 (Reuters) - New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is disbanding a police unit criticized for using excessive force against protesters in favor of a new "civilian-led approach" to large public demonstrations, he announced on Monday.

Mamdani promised in his election campaign last year to disband the police department's Strategic Response Group, a decade-old anti-terrorism unit that has faced legal challenges for its rough tactics at street protests, including the use of pepper spray by armed officers in riot gear and mass arrests.

In the joint announcement alongside New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, Mamdani said he is creating a new civilian-led group called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, whose members would be unarmed and would not have arrest powers.

At the New York Police Department, he said the disbanded SRG unit would be replaced in part by a new unit called the Patrol Support Division, which he said would police protests differently.

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," the mayor said in a statement.

A 'NOTORIOUS' UNIT

The SRG was rebuked in a 2023 legal settlement after New York Attorney General Letitia James, the New York Civil Liberties Union and others sued over excessive force against protesters, journalists and legal observers during protests against police violence in the summer of 2020.

The NYCLU and other civil rights groups cautiously welcomed Mamdani's announcement, while expressing concern that the new Patrol Support Division might end up a rebranding of the SRG, not a disbanding.

The Legal Aid Society, the city's largest public defender's office, on Monday commended the disbanding of "one of the NYPD's most notorious units" in a statement, but said the new unit "will require vigilant oversight to ensure that the SRG's tactics are not repeated."

The NYCLU said it will be "monitoring this new unit closely, including for compliance with our 2023 settlement with the City."

Tisch, who runs one of the world's largest police forces and its nearly $7 billion annual operating budget, said there were about 500 SRG officers who would be reassigned within the department before next spring. Some, she added, would go to the existing Counterterrorism Bureau.

"Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions," Tisch told ABC's Eyewitness News in a joint interview with the mayor.

A spokesperson for the mayor did not respond to queries about how the new Patrol Support Division would differ from the SRG, or whether it would be staffed by former SRG officers.

Police unions criticized the move, saying it would endanger the safety of officers and the public.

"The next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours," Patrick Hendry, president of the Police Benevolent Association, said in a statement.

Reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage and Aurora Ellis

items.title: US air travel recovery stumbles on United pause as funding fight brews
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - US air travel largely returned to normal on Monday after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days stemming from Friday's longest ground stop in 25 years, though the resumption was briefly marred by a United Airlines technology outage.

Speaking on CNBC, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy estimated the economic impact of the broader disruptions — which also delayed nearly 28,000 flights — would be in the billions of dollars. The problem was suspected to have been caused by a single router installed during routine maintenance.

United (UAL.O) on Monday experienced a technology outage affecting its departing flights for about an hour. The issue was resolved by 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT) and did not affect other airlines.

As of 6:50 p.m. ET, United had delayed 645 flights, or 20% of its schedule, and canceled 25 on Monday, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

It was unclear how many of those disruptions were caused by Monday's technology issue, as airlines were still recovering from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop.

As air travel stabilized, the conversation in Washington turned to how the air traffic control network will be fixed, how it will be funded and who was to blame for Friday's alarming shutdown.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Monday that only $4 billion of $12.5 billion approved by Congress to improve air traffic control systems had been spent. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune said.

He said just $12 billion of the $30 billion in more funding sought last week was for air traffic modernization, with the remainder for airport-related projects.

By 6 p.m. ET on Monday there were 344 flight cancellations and 4,800 delays, down from more than 2,300 canceled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware.

The four largest US airlines could face a $345 million earnings hit from the nationwide ground stop, brokerage Bernstein estimates.

FUNDING FOR UPGRADES

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that funding was needed to upgrade the air traffic control system. "Essentially, what you saw was very old equipment that had a heart attack," Trump told reporters.

Duffy on Friday raised his request for funding for air traffic control and airports to $50 billion from $30 billion. The FAA is still using aging equipment including Compaq computers, floppy disks, 25-year-old obsolete routers and paper strips to track aircraft.

"This rickety system is telegraphing to the American people, 'Hey, we need investment'," Duffy said on Monday. "Now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernize the system."

Republican Senator Eric Schmitt weighed in by saying the necessary funding was long overdue. "We should just go all in here and get this thing fixed," Schmitt told Reuters. "The can has been kicked for a long time ... Clearly this is a decades-old problem in the making."

Democrats in Congress say Duffy has spent or committed to spend just $4 billion of the initial $12.5 billion approved last year for air traffic control, while the Transportation Department said it had finalized plans for much of the funding and needs more money for telecoms upgrades.

"They have money, they don't use it, and then they come back and say, 'Give us more money.' Well, we want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it, and they don't," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said on Monday.

Democrats also want hearings into what led to the communications disruptions that brought nearly all US air travel to a halt for more than four hours on Friday.

Duffy and Republicans want quick action on the additional funding in the final weeks before the current Congress goes home and Democrats take over in January.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Kevin Liffey, David Goodman and Jamie Freed

items.title: Republican 2028 field takes shape after midterm drubbing
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The Republican Party's midterm drubbing has opened the door to a crowded battle to succeed President Donald Trump, with a wide field of potential 2028 contenders gearing up for presidential bids, according to interviews with more than a dozen people involved in prospective campaigns.

Allies and operatives around Vice President JD Vance, US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and former Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin have begun making early preparations or assessing potential campaigns, the people said.

They are "at least trying to get their ducks in order to run," said one Republican operative familiar with the activity.

More Republicans are expected to join them, according to Republican donors, strategists and influential conservative leaders, some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

Some potential candidates are also considering sitting out 2028 and waiting until 2032, calculating that Trump's unpopularity and the party's midterm losses could make the next presidential election an especially difficult one for the Republican nominee.

After those losses, many Republicans no longer view Vance as Trump's inevitable successor. While potential rivals explore bids, donors are holding back their money and some Republicans are taking a fresh look at governors who can claim distance from Washington and the Trump administration.

"What happened (in the midterms) was a major reset and changed everything as it relates to presidential politics," said Bob Vander Plaats, an Iowa evangelical leader and chief executive of The Family Leader, a conservative Christian advocacy organization.

Had Republicans fared better, "JD Vance would have been a lock in terms of the heir apparent," Vander Plaats said. Now, "he'll probably have competition and a lot of competition."

VANCE STILL THE MAN TO BEAT

Vance appears likely to run, according to four people familiar with his thinking, but has not yet formally decided as he weighs the souring political environment for Republicans and the effect of a campaign on his young family.

A Vance ally, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Vance and his political operation expected Republican figures opposed to the vice president's brand of conservatism would emerge after the midterms to promote rival presidential candidates.

The person said Vance favored a competitive primary instead of an early Trump endorsement because it would prove his mettle for a general election.

Vance would enter the race with formidable advantages as the sitting vice president with a national profile. One Republican operative who worked on a competitive House race described the nomination as Vance's to lose.

"I think if he wants the nomination, he probably wins it in an ugly fashion," the operative said, predicting a potentially nasty contest.

But running from the vice presidency could complicate his path. After largely avoiding public disagreement with Trump, Vance blamed the Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat. A week later, Trump directed him to focus on domestic issues instead of efforts to secure a peace deal with Iran.

The fallout from the conflict will likely prove a challenge for the broader Republican field, as candidates navigate how much to distance themselves from a war that Trump continues to defend.

The Vance ally said the vice president considered the midterm result a rejection of the Iran war rather than voters' verdict on the Trump presidency. When the war ends, the person said, Vance and populist Republicans will be able to rebuild Trump's coalition of voters.

CRUZ, OTHER RIVALS SEE AN OPENING

Cruz has spoken openly with associates about another White House run, after his failed attempt for the nomination in 2016, and has begun early preparations, according to two people familiar with the activity. Representatives for Cruz did not respond to a request for comment.

Over a steak dinner with conservative economist Stephen Moore before the midterms, Cruz said he planned to launch a bid, Moore told Reuters. On Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick's podcast in August, Cruz was similarly direct: "It's no secret that I want to be president."

Cruz has spent months positioning himself as a conservative who would return Republicans to a market-first domestic policy and a more traditional approach to international relations, emphasizing that any military action must be in US national interests and not aimed at nation-building.

"He says he's the mantle to the Reagan Republican wing of the party," Moore said.

One Republican donor said calls from potential candidates to major funders are likely to pick up soon, followed by donor retreats and trips to primary states early next year.

Hovering over the emerging field is Trump. He has said the Republican Party has a deep bench but suggested after the midterms that he may not endorse anyone in the primary.

Several strategists said Trump's backing could reshape the Republican nominating race.

"Unless the president swoops in with an endorsement early, there's plenty of time," said Kellyanne Conway, Trump's 2016 campaign manager and first-term senior counselor. "His endorsement is still the biggest get in all of politics."

DISTANCE FROM TRUMP MAY BENEFIT GOVERNORS

Some Republicans see a lane for conservative governors who could tout their executive experience and distance themselves from Washington and Trump's sagging popularity.

DeSantis is keeping his options open for 2028 and considering waiting until 2032, believing Trump's low approval rating could make it difficult for any Republican to win in the upcoming election cycle, according to a party operative familiar with his thinking. Florida was one of the few Republican strongholds to withstand the Democratic wave in the midterms.

Youngkin is also considering a run, according to Moore and another person familiar with his thinking. He has remained active in national Republican politics since winning the Virginia governorship in 2021 despite the state's leftward turn in recent decades. In August, he began a nationwide education advocacy group widely seen in party circles as a possible launching pad for a presidential bid.

Youngkin, whose term ended in January, supports Trump but is not seen as close to him, which could potentially help him if the party is looking for a reset.

"I know Glenn Youngkin very well and if he can find an avenue, he's likely to get in the race," Moore said.

Another potential contender is Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who three Republican donors said they hoped would enter the race.

But several people familiar with Rubio's thinking said a 2028 bid appears unlikely for now, with some close to him expecting him to spend time in the private sector. A former aide pointed instead to a possible 2032 run.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed some 45% of Republican voters said they believed Rubio would be an "excellent" presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vance.

Representatives for DeSantis, Youngkin and Rubio did not respond to requests for comment.

The early jockeying comes as some Republicans have grown pessimistic about their party's 2028 prospects.

Robert Bigelow, a major conservative donor who gave around $14 million to the main pro-Trump super PAC in the 2024 election, blamed Trump for the midterm defeats and said he expected Democrats to win the White House in 2028.

Still, Bigelow said he likes both Vance and Rubio and had suggested them as a potential ticket when Trump asked him in February who should succeed him.

Despite thinking the Democrats' election "tsunami" could last a decade, Bigelow said Vance should run.

"You can run again," he said. "But not to run at all is a mistake."

items.title: Here are the Republicans emerging as potential 2028 contenders
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 16 - Republican 2028 White House hopefuls face a difficult political landscape after President Donald Trump's party suffered a stinging midterm defeat, raising questions about whether Republican voters will rally behind candidates closely aligned with Trump or favor those charting a different course.

Will Republican voters want a Trump loyalist like Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio? Or will they prefer someone like Texas Senator Ted Cruz, who is aligned with Trump but has established his own political brand?

The following are some of the leading Republicans who are either considering a race for president or viewed as possible contenders.

VICE PRESIDENT JD VANCE

Vance, 42, a former senator from Ohio whose political career was boosted by his 2016 memoir, "Hillbilly Elegy," remains the early favorite and is seen as an eloquent defender of the "America First" principles of Trump's MAGA movement. He has said he is not sure whether he will run.

Some Republican consultants say Vance is weakened by his connection to Trump, who has a near record-low approval rating. There has been some chatter in Republican circles that he may ultimately decide to sit out 2028, though many Republicans still believe he will make a run.

Vance swiftly blamed the Republican rout in the midterm elections on the war against Iran, which was seen as a clear attempt to separate himself from Trump and the unpopular conflict.

Despite being Trump's vice president, the president has yet to make an endorsement and has signaled he may not give his backing to any candidate. "Maybe I'm better off not getting involved," Trump told CBS' "60 Minutes."

SECRETARY OF STATE MARCO RUBIO

"Whither Marco" is a frequent topic of debate in Republican circles as the 55-year-old Cuban-American has kept everyone guessing about his 2028 plans.

Some close to him rule out a 2028 run, saying he needs to make some money in the private sector after spending most of his adult life in politics, mostly as a US senator from Florida.

Rubio has largely remained above the day-to-day political fray, allowing him to avoid becoming closely identified with any one camp. But, he may be looking ahead to a 2032 run when the Trump era will be farther in the past, a former Rubio aide said.

Rubio's Hispanic roots could help the party regain support among Latino voters, one of country's the biggest bloc of swing voters, after many voted Democratic in the midterms.

Trump has at times queried Oval Office visitors on whether they prefer "JD or Marco?" and has remarked on the loud cheers that Rubio got when he traveled with Trump during the midterms.

Rubio has dismissed reports that he was considering resigning from the administration soon and has defended Trump's handling of the Iran war. He said in May that Vance would be a "phenomenal candidate" and has waved off questions about whether he harbors any ambitions for 2028.

RON DESANTIS

DeSantis, 48, who is ending his second term as governor of Florida, is viewed as a strong contender, despite failing to gain traction in 2024. DeSantis can point to the fact that his state's Republican voters held the line against the Democratic midterm wave by electing Republicans for governor and US senator.

The US Navy veteran entered the 2024 race with great fanfare, but his "Never Back Down" campaign never won broad popular support. The campaign was marked by infighting, a high burn rate of cash, and a candidate who seemed to lack people skills and tried to avoid the mainstream media.

He has criticized the "open-ended" war with Iran and called the midterm result a "close to extinction-level event for Republicans."

TED CRUZ

The longtime US senator will soon be the only statewide Republican from Texas after Democratic candidate James Talarico won a U.S. Senate seat in a stunning setback for Republicans.

Cruz, 55, has been talking to allies about a 2028 run for president and has said he does not believe the vice president is a lock for the nomination.

Cruz has run for president before. He won Iowa in 2016 before Trump's campaign gained strength and swept the field away. But that was 10 years ago, and his style as a conservative firebrand may not have the same appeal as voters look for fresh faces.

He has been a loyal ally of Trump, frequently appearing alongside him at White House events. While Trump continues to defend the Iran war, Cruz says it has dragged on for too long.

SARAH SANDERS

There is no better tell of a politician's possible aspirations for high office than when they write a book, and Sanders just published "Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy." The 44-year-old, who easily won a second term as governor of Arkansas this month, embarked on a national book tour to promote it in November.

Sanders was a press secretary for Trump in his first term and catapulted from that into the governor's mansion in Little Rock where her father, Mike Huckabee, served multiple terms.

She has steered clear of talk about running for president in 2028 by stressing she is focusing on governing her state. She has strongly defended Trump's decision to launch the Iran war.

She is popular among Trump's core base but it is unclear whether she would be able to broaden her appeal.

GLENN YOUNGKIN

The former governor of Virginia been out of office since last January but is keeping his name in the mix by promoting a national education policy group in several battleground states.

Youngkin, who has strongly defended the Iran war, has demurred on talk of a possible 2028 run, saying Vance would be a great nominee.

Youngkin, 59, has deep business experience from his career as a private equity executive. He governed as a relative moderate in Virginia, a state that has veered toward Democrats in recent elections, and could have trouble navigating a Republican primary battle usually dominated by the party's most conservative activists.

NIKKI HALEY

The former South Carolina governor frequently pops up in 2028 speculation, although recently she has been trying to tamp it down. "I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about," she told CNBC.

Haley, 54, an Indian-American, moved from the governor's seat to become US ambassador to the United Nations during Trump's first term. She drew criticism from Trump by running against him in the 2024 Republican primary race, which he won.

Haley is a more of a traditional pro-business Republican and is hawkish on foreign policy. Whether she would be able to win the support of Trump's right-wing supporters is unclear.

Reporting By Steve Holland, editing by Ross Colvin and Alistair Bell

items.title: US and Russia to oppose talks on limiting autonomous weapons
items.content_html:
GENEVA, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Major arms producers the United States and Russia look set to oppose a push at a global meeting in Geneva this week to launch negotiations on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, diplomats and rights groups said.

The rise of artificial intelligence has boosted development of drones, robots, tanks, submarines and other military hardware capable of killing without human involvement. Semi-autonomous, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East, despite ethical concerns.

The UN-hosted meeting from Monday is due to decide whether to start talks for a legally binding pact on prohibitions and regulations for Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS).

But while most of the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons support that, major military nations including the US, Russia and Israel oppose it, arguing that existing humanitarian law is sufficient.

In a video message, the UN secretary-general urged states to agree to move towards negotiating a legally binding instrument including clear prohibitions and restrictions.

"The nature of warfare is changing. New technologies – including autonomous weapon systems – present new humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges," Antonio Guterres said.

But Russia stymied the start of talks on Monday with its objection to a procedural rule allowing observers, including the EU and non-governmental organisations, to take the floor. Delegates including Ireland and Canada opposed that.

The International Committee of the Red Cross, along with the pope, has also warned of the dangers from autonomous weapons.

'DYSTOPIAN REALITY'

"Machines should never be allowed to decide who lives and dies on a battlefield but that is the dystopian reality that is fast approaching," said Verity Coyle from Human Rights Watch, which is also urging the Review Conference to take firm action.

Two diplomats told Reuters the discussions would be challenging but that a compromise may be found by the end of the week. All options are on the table, from legally binding to non-legally binding, as well as a hybrid agreement with both elements, one of the diplomats said.

Campaigners say autonomous weapons systems can behave unpredictably, raising the risk of fatal errors.

Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute – a US-based nonprofit organization focused on reducing the risks of advanced technologies, including AI – said LAWS were no longer science fiction, pointing to media reporting of early use of fully autonomous systems in Ukraine.

The US favours guidelines over binding rules on LAWS, arguing that international law already provides a framework to govern warfare. It has proposed a five-year mandate for talks towards a non-binding agreement.

Hehir told Reuters the US and Russia would probably seek to water down any outcome as they did in September with a text about autonomous weapons and their potential for harm.

The chair of this week's talks has proposed a two-year mandate to negotiate a legally binding protocol.

The UK, Germany and France propose negotiations on an instrument that leaves open whether it would be legally binding or not, Coyle told Reuters.

items.title: US DOJ warns Senator Warren about potential Trump-related probes
items.content_html:
Nov 15 (Reuters) - The US Department of Justice on Sunday warned Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, of potential "significant legal consequences" if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into President Donald Trump.

Sunday's warning is the latest sent by the Justice Department to congressional Democrats about their potential plans to investigate the administration or Trump associates.

Trump last week ordered the department to look into Democratic lawmakers for "threatening" people, and US Attorney General Todd Blanche subsequently indicated that his agency was prepared to battle congressional Democrats.

In a letter to Warren, US Attorney Aaron Reitz in Houston told the Massachusetts Democrat she appeared "eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump's private associates."

Reitz told her to preserve materials "relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights."

Notices to preserve records can presage investigations. Warren's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Reitz shared the letter on social media, and Trump reposted it to his Truth Social account several hours later.

Warren and other Democrats have signaled that when their party takes control of Congress in January, they plan to investigate large corporations, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Elon Musk, the world's richest person, among others.

OTHER LETTERS

A progressive and onetime presidential candidate, Warren is a vocal Wall Street critic and has repeatedly condemned the Trump administration and its policies.

She is the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, and is widely expected to become chair when Democrats take over Congress.

Reitz's letter to Warren cited her statements on investigating corporate leaders.

"The context sends a strong smoke signal: you intend to target private individuals close to President Trump," he wrote.

Other Democratic lawmakers who have received similar letters include Senators Richard Blumenthal and Elissa Slotkin as well as Representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee.

Political experts and Trump's opponents have raised concerns about efforts by the Republican president and his administration to target their own critics and political opponents.

Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York; Editing by Tom Hogue and Christian Schmollinger

items.title: Steering problem on tanker caused collision in New Orleans, NTSB says
items.content_html:
Nov 15 (Reuters) - The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked paddlewheel cruise boat in the Mississippi River at New Orleans last week experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, US transportation safety officials said on Sunday.

The American Cruise Lines paddlewheeler American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock. No one was killed in the collision on Friday.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was headed upriver when it experienced a "steering casualty" in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river's east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans.

NTSB officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. The tanker's voyage-data recorder was recovered on Saturday.

Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data and began analyzing information that includes bridge audio, rudder angle, propulsion performance and vessel speed, Barnum said.

Recorder data showed the asphalt tanker was traveling upriver on Friday near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. local time (1826 GMT), two minutes before the collision, when it experienced the steering issue, Barnum said.

The cruise ship capsized in about 22 minutes, NTSB officials said on Sunday. As the American Heritage toppled over into the river after the impact, harbor personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull passengers to safety.

Audio captured by the recorder included the vessel's whistle, radio warnings and requests for assistance, as well as commands to deploy anchors and other emergency ship-handling orders, he added.

Issues under investigation include whether the tanker's anchors were deployed and, if so, at what depth, as well as interviews with crew members and passengers, officials said. Interviews with the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt are scheduled over the next week, NTSB officials said.

The agency will release a preliminary report in about 30 days, the agency said.

Reporting by Siddharth Cavale in New York; Editing by Sergio Non, Will Dunham and Andrea Ricci

items.title: Fed 'has some work to do on inflation,' KC Fed chief says
items.content_html:
Nov 15 (Reuters) - The US Federal Reserve has the tools and responsibility to deal with price pressures that are "running too hot," and the central bank "has some work to do on inflation," Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeff Schmid said on Sunday.

Schmid, speaking to a credit union conference in Hawaii, did not specifically call for additional rate hikes, but said inflation is "uncomfortably above the 2% price stability target, and moving in the wrong direction."

Common narratives that have recently evolved around the nature of current inflation and the Fed's ability to contain it are off-base, Schmid said.

First, Schmid said, the view that high inflation is a reflection of repeated supply shocks neglects that "inflation is always the result of an imbalance between supply and demand. It is in the context of strong demand that a disruption to supply drives up prices. Demand always plays a role in inflation, and the Fed, through its influence on demand, always has the tools and responsibility to address inflation."

Schmid, who is not a Federal Open Market Committee voting member this year, said he also disagrees with the narrative that the sources of demand-induced inflation right now -- like the artificial intelligence buildout -- are resistant to Fed policy.

The Fed raised rates by a quarter-percentage point in September to 3.75%-4.00% but opted not to lift them again at last month's meeting.

Following recent inflation readings that were higher than expected and comments from other Fed officials, including influential Governor Christopher Waller, interest rate futures markets are now fully priced for a quarter-point increase at December's meeting, with a small probability of a half-point hike.

"I would also push back on the idea that meeting our inflation objective requires a reaction from any particular set of prices, for example prices for AI-related technology goods," Schmid said.

"Both narratives - that inflation is being driven by either supply shocks or by demand that is impervious to higher interest rates - have a common core," Schmid said. "Mainly, that inflation is somehow beyond the Fed's power to control. I don't believe this to be true. The Fed does have the tools to address inflation and has the responsibility to achieve price stability. As Chairman (Kevin) Warsh said, we have work to do."

Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci

items.title: After days of flight disruptions, officials see system back to normal by Monday
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Nov 15 (Reuters) - US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 11,500 flights affected on Sunday, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normalcy by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.

Some 2,100 flights nationwide were canceled and 9,400 were delayed on Sunday, according to aviation data site FlightAware. Airlines on Saturday had canceled nearly 6,700 US flights and delayed more than 9,100.

About 28% of JetBlue (JBLU.O) flights and 20% of American Airlines (AAL.O) flights were canceled, with United Airlines (UAL.O), Southwest and Delta (DAL.N) reporting cancellations of 3% to 5% of their flights.

The outlook for the next day was better, with just 88 Monday cancellations as of 8:28 p.m. ET (0128 GMT) on Sunday, FlightAware reported. On Saturday night, more than 875 Sunday flights had been canceled.

Duffy said on ABC's "This Week" program that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent in the matter, but the cause remained unclear. Duffy said that flights would come "back to normal" on Sunday "but probably fully normal" on Monday, and emphasized the Federal Aviation Administration's focus on keeping passengers safe.

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to US air travel since the September 11, 2001, al Qaeda attacks on the United States.

The installation by FAA contractor L3Harris (LHX.N) of at least one new router at a remote facility led to a situation in which other air traffic control centers were overloaded with a flood of data that hampered communications systems, according to officials.

Duffy said on Sunday that the replacement of a router at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other air traffic control centers across the country.

The "functionality of the originating routers" has been disabled, the FAA said on Sunday, adding that it did the same for about 60 similar routers in the air traffic control system. But the FAA still does not know what ultimately caused the problem that occurred with maintenance work that had been done thousands of times before without issue, Duffy said.

The worker who installed the router was "a good American patriot, we believe, a veteran — so we don't think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install," Duffy said. "But we don't actually have the root cause."

Two people familiar with the investigation said the router installation itself went smoothly. Any issues with the FAA's communication system developed only after the router replacement was "successfully" completed as an agency employee oversaw the work, one of the people said.

A detailed procedure of each step of the process is submitted to the FAA, they said.

Friday's problems were triggered "sometime shortly" after service at the facility was turned back over to the FAA, which had signed off on the work performed, the other person said.

Friday's disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

The routers that experienced issues were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006, Duffy said. Since Friday, Duffy has called for $50 billion in funding to upgrade air traffic control systems, up from his earlier request of $30 billion — after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year.

MORE SPENDING SOUGHT

President Donald Trump on Sunday made his first public comments on this weekend's air travel issues, also calling for additional funding from US lawmakers.

"We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," Trump wrote on social media. "Congress must approve."

Democrats are set to take control of Congress from Trump's fellow Republicans in January following their gains in the November 3 US midterm elections.

Duffy's plea for more money drew skepticism from US Representatives Rick Larsen and André Carson, the top Democrats on the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and its aviation subcommittee, respectively.

Of the $12.5 billion approved in 2025 for upgrades to the air traffic control system, about $11 billion remains unspent, Larsen and Carson said in a statement on Saturday.

"Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?" Larsen and Carson asked in their statement.

Duffy on Sunday said that the money allocated last year was earmarked only for certain spending, and did not include funds for new software to manage the airspace.

Air travel observers have also called for increased spending by private investors.

"We can't rely only on government investments. … You have to have private investment," said Justin Erbacci, director general of the Airports Council International global trade group.

Erbacci, speaking at a Montreal aviation infrastructure forum on Sunday, did not mention Friday's ground stop, but he said that investment must be made in air transport to accommodate rising traffic and outdated systems.

Global air passenger traffic is projected to more than double by 2050, according to data from airline trade group IATA.

Reporting by David Shepardson in Washington and Helen Coster in New York; Additional reporting by Allison Lambert in Montreal and Mike Stone in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non, Will Dunham and Andrea Ricci
